poem.title: The Keeper
lines: Above the harbor, where the gray gulls wheel,
A single window holds the evening light;
The keeper climbs the stair with measured heel
And trims the wick against the coming night.
No ship has asked him why he keeps the flame,
No captain knows the keeper by his name.
Yet every hull that rounds the hidden reef
Is steered by hands that never touch the wheel:
A beam, a breath, a pause, a sweeping, brief,
Unbroken signal saying what is real.
The sea forgets; the rocks remain the same;
And still he climbs, and still he guards the flame.
Some nights the fog comes in like folded wool
And smothers every star along the shore;
He sounds the horn, he keeps the lantern full,
He counts the hours and waits beside the door.
And when the morning breaks in silver seams,
He sleeps at last, and sails in other dreams—
Of ports he never saw, of lands unknown,
Of all the ships that found their way alone.

library.heading: Questions 6 through 8. Read the following passage carefully before you choose your answers.
library.intro: Placeholder introduction. The following passage is an original sample written for this practice test.
html: The town library opened at nine, but Mira arrived at a quarter to, as she had every Saturday for three years. She liked the minutes before the doors unlocked, when the street was still deciding what kind of day it would be. Delivery vans idled at the curb. A man in a paint-flecked jacket argued gently with his dog.

Inside, Mr. Abara would be walking the aisles with his cart, returning books to their places with the care of someone setting a table for guests. He never hurried, and he never seemed late; time, in that building, appeared to bend around him.

When the lock finally turned, Mira stepped in and breathed the familiar mixture of dust, paper, and floor polish. It was not that the library was quiet—children laughed in the corner, the copier clattered—but that every sound seemed to have somewhere it belonged.

directions: Section II has 3 free-response questions and lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes.
Type each response in the box next to its question. Your work is saved automatically as you type. Spelling isn’t checked, and spelling mistakes won’t affect your score.
You may pace yourself as you like, or use these suggested times: about 40 minutes on question 1, 30 minutes on question 2, and 20 minutes on question 3.

html: The following passage is an original placeholder written for this practice test. Read the passage carefully. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the author uses literary elements and techniques to convey the narrator’s complicated feelings about the town’s new bridge.

In your response, you should:
  • State a clear, defensible thesis.
  • Choose specific evidence from the passage to support your reasoning.
  • Explain how that evidence supports your reasoning.
  • Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

For forty years the ferry had carried us across the river, slow as an old argument. My grandfather ran it, then my uncle, and on summer evenings I sold lemonade to passengers who complained about the wait and then, invariably, stayed on the dock after they landed, watching the water as if it owed them something.

The bridge went up in eleven months. It was beautiful, I will admit that: a clean gray line drawn across the sky, so confident it seemed to have always been there. On opening day the mayor cut a ribbon and the high school band played something brave. People drove across, honking, and drove back, and honked again.

Nobody waits anymore. That is the whole point, and I understand it. But some evenings I walk down to the old dock, where the ferry sits with its paint peeling, and I find that I am still waiting—for what, I could not tell you.
